summary: Halometasone is a potent halogenated topical corticosteroid (commonly a 0.05% cream or ointment) used for the short-term treatment of corticosteroid-responsive inflammatory and pruritic dermatoses such as eczema/dermatitis and psoriasis. It is applied as a thin film to affected skin once or twice daily for short courses. As with other potent topical steroids, prolonged use, large surface areas, occlusion, and use in flexures or on the face increase the risk of local effects (skin atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, perioral dermatitis) and of systemic absorption with HPA-axis suppression, particularly in children. It is not FDA-approved in the United States; information here follows European SmPC/BNF-style monographs for halometasone-containing products.

moa: Halometasone is a synthetic halogenated glucocorticoid that diffuses into skin cells, binds the cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor and modulates gene transcription. This induces anti-inflammatory proteins (e.g. lipocortin/annexin-1) and suppresses pro-inflammatory mediators (phospholipase A2, cytokines, prostaglandins, leukotrienes), reducing inflammation, vascular permeability, and immune-cell activity. It also produces local vasoconstriction and antiproliferative/antipruritic effects, relieving the erythema, oedema and itch of inflammatory dermatoses.

preg: There are limited data on topical halometasone in pregnancy. As with all potent topical corticosteroids, use only if necessary, on the smallest area, for the shortest time, and avoid extensive or occluded application; prolonged/high-dose maternal topical steroids have been associated with fetal growth restriction.
lact: Topical corticosteroids are poorly absorbed with limited use, but caution is advised. Do not apply to the breast or nipple shortly before breastfeeding, and use the smallest effective amount.
renal: No dose adjustment is needed for limited topical use; systemic absorption is minimal when used appropriately.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is needed for limited topical use; systemic exposure is minimal when used as directed.

minor: Concurrent potent topical or systemic corticosteroids - additive risk of steroid effects
interactions.diagnostics: Extensive/prolonged use can suppress the HPA axis (e.g. reduced cortisol)

counsel: Apply a thin layer only to the affected skin, as directed, and avoid the face and skin folds unless told otherwise
Use it for only as long as your doctor advises - long use can thin the skin
Do not cover the treated area with airtight dressings unless instructed
Wash your hands after applying (unless treating the hands)
Tell your doctor if the rash worsens, becomes infected, or does not improve
pk: Local anti-inflammatory effect within hours to a few days of regular use
Symptom relief over several days of treatment
Minimal systemic exposure with appropriate use; not characterised as a systemic agent
Effect persists with continued use; short courses recommended

pearls: Potent/super-potent topical steroid - reserve for short courses and avoid the face, flexures and large areas
Prolonged use risks skin atrophy, striae and (with extensive use) HPA-axis suppression, especially in children
Do not use on untreated skin infections; potent steroids can mask or worsen infection
Often available combined with an antimicrobial (e.g. triclosan/fusidic acid) in some markets for infected/inflamed dermatoses
NOT FDA-approved; this monograph follows EMA/SmPC/BNF-style sources for halometasone products
missed: If you forget an application, apply it when you remember unless it is nearly time for the next; then continue as before. Do not apply extra to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: Acute topical overdose is unlikely to cause harm. Excessive, prolonged or widespread application can produce systemic corticosteroid effects (HPA-axis suppression, Cushingoid features). Management is to reduce/stop the steroid gradually and treat any adrenal suppression; large accidental ingestion is managed supportively.
